utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic, et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday. Good afternoon to the accused, to the Defence counsel, and the entire OTP team, and my greetings to the registrar and the ushers. Mr. Stringer, do you have some information for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you and good afternoon to you. Good afternoon, Your Honours and to counsel. I have prepared some remarks in response to the Trial Chamber's inquiry of yesterday with regard to the Prosecution position on the Petkovic Defence arguments on allocating or deducting time from the Defence case that is used during the examination of a co-accused witness when the examination falls outside the scope of the direct examination that's led by the co-accused. Mr. President, just a few preliminary remarks. I went back and actually looked to see what and to what extent the issue arose during the Prosecution case in chief because I think it's worth bearing in mind. We want to try to maintain consistency as between the Prosecution case and the Defence cases. And I went back through the transcript and did some searches and found that at least on three occasions during the Prosecution case, the issue arose. Back in September of 2006, witness Islamovic was testifying as a Prosecution witness; and counsel for Mr. Petkovic, actually, was questioning, and there was an objection that the questions were outside the scope of the direct examination of the Prosecution witness. I'm referring to page 6930 of the transcript. And it was actually Mr. Murphy, who was then counsel for Mr. Ostojic, intervened and pointed out that under Rule 90(h), a party may indeed question outside the scope of direct examination if the evidence goes to that party's case. I saw also that in October of 2006, the accused Praljak filed a request for additional time to cross-examine a Prosecution witness, Mr. Agic. That was filed by the Praljak Defence on the 18th of October, 2006. And shortly afterwards on the 25th of October, that Defence submission was actually joined by the Petkovic team; and in that Praljak submission, they wanted to get additional time for cross-examination of this witness, and they wanted to go outside the scope of the direct examination, and counsel for General Praljak correctly relied in his submissions on Rule 90(h)(i) as a basis for going outside the scope of the direct. And I looked at the transcript of the Trial Chamber's ruling on that, and it appears that the Trial Chamber granted the request because it granted additional time to the Praljak and to the Petkovic Defence teams to cross-examine that witness. Then thirdly, I saw that in June of 2007, during the cross-examination of Prosecution witness Marijan Biskic, again, the issue was raised. It was -- there was a Prosecution objection regarding scope of the examination. This is page 15184 of the transcript. And to be clear, the issue also related to whether leading questions could be asked when the examination was going outside the scope of the direct. But in any event, the issue was raised there; and again, Mr. Murphy was invoking or invoked Rule 90(h) indicating that Mr. Karnavas was right in asserting they could go outside the scope of the direct examination and to actually ask leading questions of the witness. So from this limited sort of survey of the Prosecution case, it raised for me, anyway, a couple of points. First of all, which was that it's clear that -- I think -- there isn't any serious disagreement that Rule 90(h)(i) does entitle any party to go outside the scope of direct examination if it's relevant to their case and obviously if the Trial Chamber agrees that it's significant or relevant enough evidence to justify doing that. The Trial Chamber has always been, it appears to me, quite consistent in its rulings on this issue. I went back and I looked at the guidelines issued by the Trial Chamber in advance of the Defence case on the 24th of April of this year. Guideline 3, paragraph 7 states that as regards the rules governing the scope of cross-examination, the Chamber recalls that pursuant to Rule 90(h)(i), cross-examination may deal with a matter that has not been raised in direct examination; and what the Trial Chamber did then was actually cite its earlier decision from the 10th of May, 2007, the decision on the mode of interrogating witnesses, in which it also made the same ruling, that a party may go outside the scope of direct under Rule 90(h)(i). However, the Trial Chamber has -- at least in my view, in the Prosecution's view until we've gotten into the Defence case, the Trial Chamber has consistently ruled is that once a party is questioning outside the scope of direct, leading questions may not be used. And I'm not going to repeat the Prosecution's submissions on the issue of leading questions during an examination of a witness by one of the co-accused; but in any event, certainly in our view the Trial Chamber has consistently approved the practice and has on specific occasions allowed this to occur, of course, during the Prosecution case as well as in the Defence cases. I think that it's worth pointing out that on those occasions during the Prosecution case in chief when counsel for the Defence were allowed to go outside the scope of the Prosecution direct examination under Rule 90(h), there was no deduction of time from any of the Defence cases, and of course, that's because there were no Defence cases and no times to deduct from. So right off the bat, I think that's a point that bears keeping in mind because I know that one of the assertions from the Petkovic Defence is that it's unfair for the Prosecution to be allowed to go beyond the scope of direct now under Rule 90(h) and to not have that time deducted from its overall time. The fact is that that same rule was in effect during the Prosecution phase of the case. The Defence were allowed to do that, and there was no deduction from the Defence, obviously. But it's possible that -- at least in our view, the other point on this that's maybe the most significant to bear in mind, and I don't know that there's going to be a lot of disagreement on it, during the Prosecution case and from what we've seen so far in the Defence cases, it's our submission that this issue really doesn't raise a statistically -- or it doesn't involve a statistically significant amount of time. On those occasions when a party has wanted to go outside the scope and to proceed with new questions under Rule 90(h), you know, I could be wrong. There may be disagreement, but I think we are talking about 10 minutes here, 20 minutes there, but not in the grand scheme of things statistically significant amounts of time, and I'll come back to that because that's largely what drives the Prosecution's ultimate position on this. In regard to the Petkovic assertion that it's unfair for time to be deducted from the Petkovic Defence while there's no corresponding deduction from the Prosecution time since our case is over, there are three points we'd make. First, we think it's not unfair to do that because, as I've already pointed out, time wasn't deducted from the Defence cases back during the Prosecution case. When they went outside the scope, there was no deduction of time of the Defence cases because, as I said, there were no Defence times during that phase of the case. Secondly, as the Trial Chamber knows, the reason for allowing a party to go outside the scope of direct and to raise new questions is to prevent the witness from having to come back; and with six accused in the case, it's theoretically possible that any of the Defence witnesses could ultimately be required or asked to come back several times if there was not a situation where a co-accused could go outside of the scope of the direct. Clearly, if the Petkovic team wanted to bring back a witness called by the Prlic Defence, they could do so. However, of course, we know that if that were to happen, that time would be deducted from the Petkovic Defence. So it seems, again, not unfair to simply deduct the time now that the witness is here. And thirdly, as the Trial Chamber knows - I'm not going to belabour it - the Prosecution view, and we've said it a number of times both orally and in written submissions, we do view the cross-examinations conducted by the Defence teams to be cross-examination only by label for the large part in that these are largely sympathetic or certainly not adverse witnesses. And so we do see it as a different situation than the situation you have when the Prosecution is cross-examining Defence witnesses. So for those three reasons, we think it's not unfair that the Trial Chamber continues to deduct time from a Defence team that goes beyond the scope of cross-examination. Now, so our ultimate position on is this is as follows: Mr. President, we recognise that this is not a perfect situation, but the status quo, if you will, is what we are advocating; that is, these are very factual driven decisions and findings that are made by the Trial Chamber whenever a party -- whenever there's an objection on scope, and if the party is or is not within the scope of the direct examination when they're asking their questions, it's a complicated issue. It's very factually driven, and it's not one that lends itself easily at all to any sorts of firm or set rules or guidelines. We think that it's appropriate for the Trial Chamber on a very case-by-case basis to decide whether questions are outside the scope of direct or not; and if so, we continue to assert that the Trial Chamber is correct in deducting that extra time from a Defence team that does go outside the scope of the direct examination. But getting back, really, to the main point, so far we don't think that this is a statistically significant amount of time. And if I may, in using the Petkovic Defence as an example because they're the ones that have raised it, if at the end of the Petkovic case in chief, after they have exhausted their 50 hours or their 55 hours of time, if it turns out that there are a few hours that they need that they don't have because the Trial Chamber had deducted those few hours from their time when they were cross-examining other witnesses and went outside the scope, there's nothing to prevent the Petkovic team from at that point making an application to the Trial Chamber to make up that time for more time. The Trial Chamber has always been very flexible in administering all of these rules. The Prosecution asked for more time at the end of its case in chief. Time was granted. We didn't use it, all of it, but certainly I think that when you're talking about 15 minutes here, 20 minutes there, in the end it's not going to add up to a huge amount of time that will impact ultimately the length of the trial in any real significant way. And in any event, any of the teams can ask for that time back, and if they can make their showing to the Trial Chamber, I'm confident the Trial Chamber will give them the amount of time they need. But that's how we propose is the way to go, to continue doing it the way the Trial Chamber's been handling it so far, deducting time when it finds that there is questioning beyond the scope of direct, and if at the end the Defence team needs to try to recover that time in order to complete their case in chief, then they can apply to the Trial Chamber for that additional time. Mr. President, just three last remarks, and these don't relate to this specific issue, but rather, just to some of the other points that surfaced in yesterday's proceedings because it seems to us, the Prosecution, that the calendar and scheduling for the remainder of the year is certainly in flux now. Could we confirm, if possible, that the week that had been envisioned for the expert witness Mr. Cvikl, that that week of November 17th is an empty week and that it's not going to be filled. Secondly, we would encourage the Trial Chamber to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it can be filled with a witness Radovanovic. We asked for your position regarding this witness because we've already got the report. He is a demographer, an expert in demography. It's not too complicated, so possibly he could testify in that week from the 17th -- or she could come and testify in the week of the 17th to the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, with respect, to the Prosecution would object to that. It's -- we're still reviewing the report. It's our intention to file our RULE 94 bis response to the report, and it's our view that Ms. Radovanovic cannot be moved forward earlier in time. Prosecution can't be prejudiced by having just received the report and being pushed into an examination sooner than we are ready. We've got 30 days under rule 94 bis to file our response to the report. We think it's time that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I can listen to you, but I read the report this morning, and I can demonstrate to you that I, I can cross-examine her without any problem for 2 to 3 hours. I do not need a whole month to know what questions to put to her, or the more so since we've already had Ms. Tabeau who came to testify on demographic problems that we are all aware of. Of course, as per the rules, you have 30 days to respond. You can. But you could also show some cooperation since there's a gap in the calendar, and you could say at least that this expert can come. There can be examination-in-chief by the Defence with possibly postponement of the cross-examination if you are overwhelmed by the questions that are put. But you are a very great professional, and I don't think that you're going to be hindered by the situation. If that expert can come and testify in the week from the 17th to the 20th, a big problem is then solved. And secondly, if you are very prompt with regard to the eight 92 bis witnesses, if you state your position saying I want to cross-examine this one and that one, then Mr. Karnavas can be told straightaway, and he can have them be called for that week as well, and all the problems are solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I know the demographics are foremost in your mind today because you've been listening to evidence of that throughout the morning session. With respect, it's the Prosecution position, Mr. President, that the Prosecution will not be prepared to examine Ms. Radovanovic prior to the week that she's scheduled for, which is the final week of November. I understand that the Trial Chamber wishes us to have a different position, and I regret that we're not able to agree. Obviously, the Trial Chamber is the Trial Chamber, and we will abide by whatever order it issues. But we think it's unfair to railroad us, frankly, into having to proceed with our examination of what we view as an important demographic expert. If I could -- just to continue, we also wanted to encourage the Trial Chamber if possible to set a deadline. I don't know when counsel is planning to file his rule 92 bis motions. We are anxious to see those and to file a prompt response, and we think that that would facilitate all of the witness calendaring; and that was our third request, was whether it's possible to get witness calendars from both the Prlic and Stojic teams for November and December, at least proposed ones, because everyone knows that there's a great deal of uncertainty. But if we could have some calendars and names that are at least on the table, I think it would assist all of us in preparing the Prosecution's concern about having - as appears to be the case with the expert Radovanovic - having to prepare cross-examinations and being pressured to prepare its cross-examinations at the last minute or under less, you know, than ideal conditions. And we think that's unfair, and we think that if we had some potential or some proposed calendars and if we had counsel's rule 92 bis motion, it would certainly put us in a better position to prepare ourselves for the remainder of this year's proceedings. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, today is the 21st of October, unless I'm mistaken. Yes, 21st of October. The 21st of November, that is a month away from now. You have more than enough people in your team. Don't tell me that you don't have somebody in your team who can prepare for a whole month based on the report that you have for the cross-examination. I find it hard to believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We do have someone who can prepare, and I can assure you that the preparations are underway. I guess -- and I think you know, Mr. President, that I and all of us on the Prosecution team are always anxious to try to facilitate the proceedings and to accommodate the parties and the Trial Chamber. We just got the report yesterday, and I know that you've read it, Mr. President. To be perfectly honest, I have not. I've been having to do other things. But I led the evidence of Ewa Tabeau when she testified in this case, and the demographic part of the case is important to me, and I would like to have an opportunity to read the report, and it's possible that our position would change. But I'm being abundantly cautious at the moment because I've not reviewed the report, and I'm also troubled by the fact it was, in our view, filed late without giving us enough time to prepare and to consider what our position would be on it. I can't tell you what our -- it may be that there are parts of it we accept or that we -- we don't have strong objection to or that we -- it may be that it's not complicated, as you suggest, Mr. President, but at the moment I've not read it, and so I'm not really comfortable making any concessions on the timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Stringer, you could do one thing: Read the report without delay, and tell us whether you are in a position or not because you are going to be the one cross-examining Ms. Radovanovic, I suppose. You can read the report, see what the problem is, and within a fortnight or in two weeks' time, ask for another date or to ask whether the 27th of November is okay. We depend on you. You are the one who can tell us whether you are able to because you were the one asking questions of Ms. Tabeau; therefore, you are the number one in the Prosecution team when it comes to demographics. So very quickly, you'll be able to tell us whether you can or not or whether you need further time. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Did you have another topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon. Good afternoon to you. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. If I may just be allowed a single minute to reply to the words of my learned friend, Mr. Stringer, about cross-examination, Defence cross-examination in relation to two issues that weren't raised in chief. First of all, in any legal matter when an accused is trying to stand up because one of his rights have been violated, at least in his opinion, the extent of this violation or purported violation is not in itself of any substance whatsoever. Therefore, it does not in the least matter whether Petkovic's overall time for the presentation of the Petkovic Defence would be taken away from in terms of time to a large extent or to a small extent. The next question is, does an accused have the right to raise other issues on cross-examination that weren't raised in chief? I'm also very glad that the OTP and the Petkovic Defence agree entirely on their interpretation of Rule 90(h). We therefore believe that there is now no doubt about the fact that both the Defence and the OTP have the right on cross-examination to go into issues that go beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief. My third remark, what remains in doubt is whether such examination by Defence teams should be considered as cross-examination length-wise or if this is miraculously transformed somehow into an examination-in-chief and therefore deducted from the time allocated to a Defence team. I would like to draw everyone's attention to the fact that no one in this courtroom has so far come up with any objections or, indeed, observations to the effect that the subjects that I used in my examination of the witness were subjects outside the scope of the examination-in-chief. I would also like to draw everyone's attention to Rule 90(h)(iii). The Trial Chamber has the power to allow or disallow the questioning of a witness on other subjects. I believe that by making no ruling at all on my cross-examination, the Trial Chamber either believed that my examination was in no way outside the scope of the chief or tacitly agreed to have me proceed as I did. One thing that cannot be disputed is that the decision rendered by this Trial Chamber on the right to cross-examine outside the scope of the chief is something that must be adopted ahead of time so that any Defence that takes this approach can decide under what circumstances they will be adopting this approach or, indeed, dropping this approach. It is by no means possible for any rule known to this court to have the situation as follows: A part of the cross-examination by a Defence outside the scope of the chief to not be treated as cross-examination while any time used for such examination is deducted from a Defence's overall time. By way of a conclusion, General Petkovic's Defence does not believe that the most important issue is the issue of equal treatment for both the OTP and the Defence. Rather, we believe that what is at stake here is the just nature of this trial, the application of the rules, and especially in this case, Rule 90(h). Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... and the situation in the days to come rest on the shoulders of Mr. Karnavas, so he will have to tell us how many 92 bis witnesses will come and testify - four or more, we don't know - after the 13th of November. For the time being, there's nothing during the week of the 17th of November and the 24th of November, also, since Mr. Stringer wishes to cross-examine the witness at a later stage. So there are two weeks ahead of us that could be used to hear the 92 bis witnesses or their evidence, so we need to have the list very quickly to know which witnesses can be called. Otherwise, we will have a gap since Cvikl cannot be translated before the 22nd of December, which means that Cvikl's testimony will not start before the 12th of January when the court is back in session, the week from the 12th to the 16th. So we will hear Cvikl, and the week after that we will hear the first witness of the Stojic Defence team. This is how things stand. I stand to be corrected, however. Mr. Karnavas, is this how you see things also?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. I'll be very brief and very blunt. First, with respect to the four 92 bis witnesses that have been previously cross-examined by the Prosecutor in previous cases, they, especially they - and I mean Mr. Stringer and Mr. Scott - know exactly who they want to call. They know the testimonies; they know what they testified. Essentially, we want to introduce their prior testimonies. So they can tell us very easily without being so coy as to which one of these witnesses they wish to call. That would eliminate some of the guessing that's going around. Second of all, with respect to the other four witnesses, as I indicated, I'm still waiting for one of the statements. We did receive the third one today. We hope to have that by the end of the week. As far as the expert demographer, and let me just remark the following: They have an entire demographic team. The two reports, one is about 25 pages at best if you stretch it. The other one is about ten pages. The reports are an analysis of their expert reports. So when you consider they have several demographers, an entire demographic team behind them, plus an armada of Prosecutors, I find it, frankly, incredibly troubling to hear that a month is insufficient to determine whether they're capable of cross-examining this particular expert. Now, the problem with this particular expert is that she is also a professor, so we would like to have that testimony taken this year if possible. We would urge the Court to force the Prosecutor to come up to speed. Frankly, had I received this report on Sunday night or Monday morning, I would have read it by now, especially when the Trial Chamber invited the Prosecutor for their remarks today. One would think that they would at least glance at it. So I do think that perhaps the Trial Chamber should force the Prosecutor and give them a deadline to look at it and come back. And I don't believe and I take offence to the remark that was made - perhaps it was made in haste - that somehow the Trial Chamber is trying to railroad the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber is merely trying to exercise its discretion and trying to push this trial along as expeditiously as possible. Lastly, on the one issue that was raised concerning Ms. Alaburic's motion, I must say that I found the Prosecutor's remarks very balanced, and I believe that the ultimate -- the ultimate conclusion which was at the end of the case, the Trial Chamber would have an opportunity to assess whether the lawyers were efficient and whether they do need some additional time because it would be reasonable. I think that's an adequate solution. And I think far too much time is being spent on this issue. We're spending more time debating this issue than actually time being spent questioning outside the scope. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I just raise one question, Your Honour, which occurs to me to arise out of all this, which is that when Mr. Karnavas is finished his case, if he comes to conduct this sort of examination of other Defence witnesses, how would the adjustment be made of his time? Because he will have finished his case, so he will be in the same position as the Prosecution. So I'm just wondering -- it's just a question, really, how it's all going to work then because some sort of equality of treatment among the Defence teams is also presumably inherent in the Trial Chamber's thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's why we've been asked to reserve time. We were allocated a certain amount of time, and we're reserving about eight hours. So that should make sure that none of the Defence are going to be treated disproportionately somehow; the first team is going to have the advantage. In fact, I would dare say the first team has a disadvantage above everybody else because we have to prepare in a less amount of time and try to manage our case, especially this type of a case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Ms. Alaburic. This is what I had understood. Mr. Karnavas since he did not have all his 95 hours had set aside a few hours in case such a situation arose. That is the answer he has given you, but that is what I had understood. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that my learned friend Mr. Karnavas should find this a simple task because in order to present his case, he was given just slightly under twice the time of some of the other Defence teams. What I would like to draw your attention to is this: One issue is additional time being granted for hearing the witnesses of other Defence teams. This is beyond dispute, and this is something that has already been applied in this courtroom. We'll take some of the time and allocate it to our Defence to additionally hear certain other witnesses. This is something that no one is trying to challenge. What we are talking about here is additional issues within the bounds of time already allocated for cross-examination. So let's say I have 20 minutes for my cross-examination. The question remains whether within those 20 minutes I have the right under Rule 90(h) to broach other issues as well. And what if I wish to ask additional questions in relation to these 20 minutes allocated to me? Of course, I will have to use up some of the time that has been allocated to the Petkovic Defence team. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few remarks in response to counsel. Yes, we know who four of the eight -- well, we know who all the witnesses are in the 98 bis, and four of them have testified here before, and we know who they are. And I said yesterday, we can file a response very fast. We're not being coy. We just need the motion. Just file the motion, and we'll respond, and we can all move forward. That's the point. We don't file motions. We don't make motions like this orally. Put the paper into the registry, and we'll file our response, and we can all move ahead. That's as simple as it needs to be. It doesn't have to be nasty, and it doesn't have to be coy, and we're not being coy. We just want to have a motion to respond to. That's all. I'm not suggesting, Mr. President, that the Trial Chamber is trying to railroad the Prosecution. I think it's evident that the Prlic Defence has tried to railroad the Prosecution in respect of these two experts. Both of these reports have been filed months after a deadline. We've talked about this before, and I know the Trial Chamber doesn't seem to be troubled by that. But again, none of this can work to the prejudice of the Prosecution, and that's -- all we're doing is trying to protect ourselves and give ourselves the ability to prepare having received both of these reports very late -- very late in the game. So those are my only remarks, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, of course the Trial Chamber is concerned. Of course we have realized that these reported had not been filed as had been said in March and April. Of course we contemplated the possibility of dismissing these reports because the deadlines had not been abided by. But we also took into account issues that related to the work of the Defence team, that have a heavier workload, that don't have the same resources as you do, that find it more difficult to get ahold of these experts, so all of this is quite complicated. After having spent a lot of time thinking about this, we felt that in the interest of justice it would be preferable in the future that all expert reports for those upcoming witnesses be filed at least two months ahead of time, two months before the witness in question comes to testify in order to abide by the 30-day deadline of the 94 bis rule of our rules of procedure in evidence. So in the future, it has to be two months. Of course we are concerned about it. The Trial Chamber is trying to put both parties back on track because if everybody derails, then it's a disaster. This is why we suggest guidelines. We are trying to do our best. Our last topic, Mr. Karnavas -- Mr. Karnavas, on Thursday the 30th of October, could we possibly switch from the morning to the afternoon? This is an application made by the Seselj Chamber. Could we possibly switch and sit in the afternoon and not in the morning as planned?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We would be more than happy to accommodate Mr. Seselj in the Seselj Chamber. That would not be a problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we will sit on the 30th of October in the afternoon. Let's bring the witness in, and I shall tell the witness that we have been involved in procedural matters. We need a few IC numbers. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One of the parties have submitted his objection to the list of documents tendered by the Prosecution through witness Zelenika, Mirko. These objections submitted by the Prlic Defence team have been given Exhibit number IC 00868. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. You have been waiting since quarter past 2.00. I'm sorry, but we have had to deal with a some of procedural matters. And we were not able to call you in. I apologise for this and for having made you wait, but we could not do it any other way. According to the registrar's calculations, you should have one hour and 50 minutes left, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe I have slightly less than that, Your Honour. I believe it's an hour and 5 minutes or something to that effect, but...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was overgenerous with you as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think we will be finished perhaps as early as a half an hour from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could go back to where we were yesterday in that last -- we are at the second-to-last, penultimate chapter on distribution of humanitarian aid; and if I could focus your attention on document 1D 00303. And when you have it, let me know.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have located the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, this concerns the Livno municipalities dated 11 May 1993. Have you had a chance to look at it prior to coming to court, this document, during the proofing session?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but not before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not before that. Now, in looking at this particular document, we can see that the humanitarian -- the criteria set out by the Livno municipalities, can you tell us whether looking at what is being done in the Livno whether Mostar was doing the same thing, setting criteria, that is for the humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The coordinating committee in cooperation with the social welfare centre worked on setting up these criteria, and the records were set up according to the rules that we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Is Livno doing anything differently than what Mostar is doing at this time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that the quantities allocated for distribution were different in viewing the overall amount of humanitarian aid received. Anyway, all distribution criteria were based on the availability of the aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me focus your attention now for illustrative purposes on Article 28, Roman numeral XXVIII. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: From here we can see that it sets out certain criteria, 5 kilograms of flour per person in a household and so on and so forth. Are we to understand that Mostar had similar criteria, these sorts of items?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially since this reminds me of the criteria that the ICRC applies, and a little below -- anything below that would be insufficient for distribution. So these are minimum quantities and minimum criteria applicable to distribution to either families or individuals to satisfy the minimum needs that they have in a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you indicated this would be minimum distribution. What if - hypothetical - what if in your warehouse you have various items, but because of the number of people that you need to distribute the aid to, you cannot meet the minimum distribution per person? What happens then?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we have a problem, and we would solve this problem in a variety of ways. We would look at the plan for the forthcoming influx of aid, if we had any notices thereof, and then we would postpone the distribution pending the arrival of these forthcoming quantities. If we were not certain that humanitarian aid would arrive any time soon, then we would conduct the distribution according to priorities, but then again, not below the minimum quantities required for sustenance, the ones that are presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, yesterday, we talked about the situation in Mostar in April and May, and you had indicated based on the charts that we saw that collectively, the coordinating committee had very few resources available for distribution; and you also indicated from your notes that there were some 30.000 displaced persons in Mostar, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let's say now, hypothetically speaking, that you only have enough for 15 or 20.000. Why not -- why not distribute to all but distribute less than the minimum quantity as prescribed by the criteria, so at least, then, everybody gets a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that such distribution would only cause dissatisfaction among beneficiaries, and that would cause the situation to deteriorate because as much as those people were needy, they were still unwilling to be treated subhumanely, so we took very good care not to create additional problems for these people, not to offend them by offering them such meager quantities. So any distribution in such minor quantities would be seen by them as humiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next document, 1D 02763. 1D 02673. And in this particular document, we see various certificates. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You can see at the top of the page, Social Welfare Centre Mostar, 24 May 1993 on the very first one, and perhaps on some of the others we have the same date. This Social Welfare Centre Mostar, this is the municipality of Mostar, social centre, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in looking at -- let's look at the first certificate. Maybe you can help us out here. This certifies a Mr. Izet Curic, that he is an employee of the Mostar Social Welfare Centre and employed as a social worker. Did you know this individual?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us what a social worker did within the social welfare centre? Concretely, what were the sort of tasks that social workers were doing?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this certificate is not actually a certificate or a proof. These were actually issued to employees of the social welfare centre in order to allow them to go into the field to assess the situation and the needs there and to analyse the method of distributing humanitarian aid in cooperation with people from humanitarian organisations operating in local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So they were employees of the social welfare centre; and at the same time, based on this certificate as proof, they were allowed to go out into the field and to assess the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, yesterday we saw the chart, and you discussed a little bit about how the food was ultimately distributed at the commune level: People got cards, they would come to the commune centre, and then they would receive their aid. Am I stating your testimony correct from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now you're telling us that individuals such as Mr. Curic as a social worker would go into the field and make assessments. Would he be making assessments at the commune level to see whether particular individuals met the criteria in order to get the card so that they could go to the commune when food was being distributed?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the main task was precisely that, which is that in cooperation with the local commune commissioner, he assesses a situation as a professional and check whether the aid was received by those who have properly certified cards, whether there are some newcomers who need to be given a status and issued with a card. So the whole process of validity and confirmation of the cards was under the supervision of this person from the social welfare centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And by looking at the name, and of course you know the gentleman, can you tell us whether he was a Croat or a Muslim or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the name he was a Muslim; but since I know him personally, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's just look again at the second certificate. This is for a Mr. Fehim Sunagic. He's also a social worker. This is again dated 24 May 1993. Did you know this individual?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What nationality is he?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same like the previous one, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the next certificate, again, dated 24 May 1993, a Mr. Mehmed Buric?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's also a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you know this individual?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he was doing the same work as the others that were doing, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then we have a Ms. Elvira Colic. She is employed as a protocol officer. Did you know Ms. Colic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And what's written here as a description of what she did is correct. I know that this is what she was doing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us what a protocol officer does or did back then?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Keeping records of incoming mail, making categorization of cards received by the centre to be verified and certified, and all other supporting documents that were delivered to that institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is this individual Muslim or Croat?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was also a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next certificate [French interpretation], is she a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [French interpretation] She was also a Muslim, and I had many a cup of coffee that she made for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about the next certificate, a Ms. Hata Colic [French interpretation]?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same. This lady was a Muslim, and she did the same job as the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then we go on again, the next certificate is [French interpretation] Pervan [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what did she -- she's -- you can see that she is a social [French interpretation]?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were 32 local communes in Mostar, which required a large number of people to be out in the field monitoring the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And finally, the last certificate, 26th of May, 1993. Do you see this name to know whether this is a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a Muslim woman, since this is a female and the status and the reason for issuing this certificate was the same; only the time frame was different. If anyone was required to go out, they had to have this kind of certificate on themselves in order to prove that they are authorised social workers working in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we request go on to the next document, 1D 02771.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Witness, I have three questions for you. I think they are relevant based on these eight documents that we've just seen. I noticed that for most of the documents, they were written on the 24th of May, 1993; but for the last one, that was drawn up on the 26th of May, 1993. We know that all the people mentioned in the documents are Muslims. You told us that you knew them because you discussed things with them. You even said that you would take -- you would have coffee with one of them. Based on this, I have three series of questions. So these are Muslims working in the social work centre. Where did they live? Did they live in East or West Mostar? Where did these people live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were living in West Mostar, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So they were living in West Mostar. Most of the certificates concern women. I suppose these women had husbands; they were married. Did these women speak about their husbands? What did they do? What was their occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I don't know. There were men, as well, on this list, but I don't know their personal situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you did not know their personal situation in any detailed manner? You talked about their work with them, I suppose, about their lives, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I didn't have time to discuss their lives with them. We always only talked about work during working hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. But when you would discuss with them, would they mention the problems that there were at the time? Did they, for instance, say that they at any point in time they had learned that Muslims had been arrested, had been transferred to Heliodrom? Did they speak to you about it, or were these topics you would never speak about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't discuss those things with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were working in West Mostar, and you said they also lived there. Could they move about freely, or would they come up with problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. They had no problems moving around. They would come to work, go out into the field, and the purpose was these certificates to allow them to go out into the field, so they had absolute freedom of movement. If Your Honours would like to know, I could tell you that at the time in West Mostar, there were about 8.000 Muslims, 2 and a half thousand Serbs, and about 1.000 others in addition to 30-odd-something-thousand Croats, and these figures are more or less accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. From what you say, back then in May, say, in West Mostar, there were 8.000 Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many Croats in West Mostar, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 30.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. 30.000, you said so. So there were 8.000 Muslims moving around without any problem; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. They were beneficiaries. Anyone who was capable of doing work or becoming engaged, they were engaged, and they were doing all sorts of work; and there were no problems in that respect. And this was already a time when the situation was somewhat normalised as compared to the initial stage when the conflict started; but as time went on, the situation progressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there men, women, children among the 8.000 Muslims? The children - for instance, the children of your employees - would they go to school or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the schools were open, yes, but I can't remember now whether schools were working at the time or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You do not know whether the schools were working? Did you yourself -- did you have children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My children were with my mother and father in Peljesac in Croatia as refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No because if you told me that you had children --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, lots of women and children had left the war zone and become refugees, and that took place at the very beginning when the conflict broke out in April 1992 in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes. Another question. Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, two small questions. Could you remind me, how many people were employed in this social centre in Mostar in May 1993? We've just seen eight certificates, but I'd like to know how many altogether there were there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just give you an approximate answer, but I think that there were up to 30 employees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So out of 30 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But not more than 30, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So these eight certificates for Muslims, is that the overall number of Muslims working in the centre, or were you just giving us some examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. These were the people who were required to go out into the fields; and in view of the overall situation and the need for them to cooperate with the local commune staff, they were issued with these certificates in order to allow them to go out into the field. The other employees who didn't need to go out normally came to their offices and did their job at the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just one more question: What was the, say, political affiliation of the people employed in the centre? In other words, did the employer, the centre as such, did it know the political affiliation of every employee? Did they know what political party they would belong, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that I'm able to give you an answer to this question. I just met these -- with these people within our work and the scope of our work, and I knew nothing about their political affiliations or any thoughts that they might have on this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very last question. We have seen the certificates, mostly delivered to female employees. If these women were married, did some of them have Muslim husbands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I absolutely don't know who they were married to. That was their personal affair, and I can say nothing about that. All I can say, that there were lots of mixed marriages in Mostar, Muslims married to Croats or -- Muslim men married to Croat women and vice-versa, but I don't know anything about these particular cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You've answered my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we turn to the next document, 1D 2771. And the next few documents, in fact, are more or less the same with the exception of the last document in this bundle. This document, we see that there's a list of welfare beneficiaries, and it's dated 25 June 1995. We see that at the top. Do you know for what period of time this list was for?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I look at the date on this document, this appears to be June 1993, possibly May or June. I think June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It must be a translation error on my part or in the English version. Okay. Now, looking at this document very briefly, I know we've looked at it together, and there is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you're right. In the English translation, it's dated 1995; but if you look at the original, I see 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at this document, there are 70 names. Can you tell us by looking at the names whether within this list you have Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than 25 if my count is correct. 28, a total of 28, I think, that I've come across.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just as a representation, for instance, number 3, number 6, number 7, number 10, number 12, number 15, number 16, number 17: These are all Muslim names, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We won't go through the rest. If we look at the next document, 1D 02769, do you recognise this document, and if so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another list of eight beneficiaries in a different local commune. This was drawn up to indicate categories of aid as well as a status of beneficiaries and then various groups of those. The document is quite complete, thorough. It has all the information: address, father's name, name, ethnicity. It's all reflected in this document, and it's crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's dated 16 August 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, who would have prepared this document? Who was responsible for preparing this document?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was drawn up by the governing commissioner for this local commune in cooperation with commissioners of the social welfare centre and commissioners of the humanitarian organisations who worked in these local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we know at the time - that is August 1993 - you were still with the Red Cross. Would you have come across this document or this sort of a document in your work?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an associate who worked with humanitarian aid who would have known about a document like this because he checked the status and distribution of humanitarian aid and cross-referenced them with lists drawn up by commissioners across local communes. Based on the final result in terms of how many beneficiaries there were, we would distribute aid. So this associate of mine probably had a chance to look at all these documents in each of the local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next two documents, 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- the next two documents, 1D 02768 and 2774. These are more or less the same sort of lists, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the distinction being this is a new local commune with new names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, what about 1D 02770 dated 31 August 1993? It says "list families of civilian victims of the homeland war." Can you please tell us what this list is about, or is it somewhat similar to the ones that we have seen already?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is a different kind of category. People who suffered in the war. They were also, in a way, jeopardized and therefore were entitled to special aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the final document in this chapter, 1D 02659. 2659. This is a report on work in 1994. If you look at the end of this report, before we get to the chart, we see your name as president. That would have been president of the Red Cross of the municipality of Mostar, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I assume since it bears your name and signature that you would have been responsible for the preparation of this particular report?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I had to submit a report every year to the assembly of the Red Cross on the work of the Red Cross over the previous year. If you look at this report, particularly in relation to the one that we looked at yesterday, you can observe a continuity in the work of the Red Cross, a continuity in its work across a number of different areas. Furthermore, there is new information here about newly arisen situations in 1994. This report shows a somewhat improved situation as compared to the previous year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course, if we look at the last page, the chart, we can see that the food or the resources that were available month per month are relatively good compared to what we saw in 1993, at least that one period of April and May 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what it shows. This list is about the rate of arrival of food in Mostar Red Cross in 1994. I sort of missed the list in relation to the first six months because if we had that, we would be able to see that there was sufficient aid. The quantities are no longer as they were back in 1993 in the thick of the war. The quantities of aid were also reflection of the trust in the work of the Red Cross, the transparency of its activities, the quality of both reception and distribution. This is one thing that I can state with the greatest amount of certainty. If you look at this report, you can see that on a daily basis there were over 32 tonnes of various kinds of aid passing through. These are no negligible quantities. In addition to its ambition to have aid distributed to everyone, the Red Cross was facing a great deal of trouble, and it required a huge effort to accomplish all of these tasks in the best possible way. Needless to say, we could not have done this alone. There were local commune commissioners always at hand to get their men and go and get help, representatives of the civil protection who helped us load and unload aid. There were various activists as well as employees of the Red Cross who went about their work on a regular basis. They would monitor the situation, incoming goods, goods being distributed, as well as anything else included in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Unless there are any questions from the Bench, I'm going to move to the final chapter of my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one minor question. We've just seen this report. It concerns the year 1994. With regard to the previous year, is there a similar report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may refresh everyone's memory, we saw that yesterday, but we can go back to that if you wish to make some comparisons; and that would be number 2651, Your Honour. That would have been the -- I believe the third chapter of the list of documents, and that was where we looked at some of the charts yesterday, if you may recall, for the various months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The reason why I was asking you this is that I had not forgotten about Document 2651, and I think that for the year 1994 you chose another format, is that right, to show your activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's obvious if you cross-reference the two documents, but the substance remains the same. There were different sectors in the work of the Red Cross, and reports were submitted in relation to each of these in a slightly abbreviated form. Later reports in relation to 1995, 1996, and on for as long as I was still with the Red Cross were much shorter. None of the activities and tasks performed were ever omitted, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the time has come for the break. We're going to break now, and you can deal with your last chapter after the break. Let's break for 20 minutes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Judge Prandler has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yesterday, we have already talked about the international relationship as far as the Red Cross movement is concerned and the Red Cross Red Crescent movement, and I would like to revisit that problem and ask you, Mr. Simunovic, the following question. Just before we adjourned, the report, your report of the activities of the municipal organisation of Red Cross Mostar in 1993 had been mentioned by Mr. Karnavas; and then if we look at the report in English translation of it, then we will see that the -- Red Cross Mostar in the major heading, Red Cross Mostar, then Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then Red Cross of Croatia, Republic Herceg-Bosna, and then again township organisation Mostar. Now, my question is about the following, that the -- as we also mentioned yesterday, as a rule, the international Red Cross and Red Crescent movement accepts one organisation from and in each country, and we have here in the title Bosnia and Herzegovina, but as a republic, of course, I assume, at the same time the name of your organisation is being mentioned here as Red Cross of Croatia, Republic Herceg-Bosna. The question is, was that organisation as such and your name officially accepted by both, by the international committee of Red Cross, that is ICRC, and by the International Federation of the Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies? I'm interested in this question also from the point of view of my own experience that at that time in Hungary and Budapest the regional delegation of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies had been established just for dealing with -- mainly with the problems which were created by the tragic events in former Yugoslavia. So my question is, therefore, that was there any official recognition by the two mentioned international organisations, that is ICRC and the international federation of your organisation? Did you have any - quote, unquote - "official" contacts with them, and did you have, for example, contacts with their Geneva-based centres and organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for this question, Your Honour. I can expand at great length on this subject since I have witnessed all the developments surrounding the transformation of the Red Cross in Bosnia-Herzegovina starting with Day 1 and my arrival in Mostar, all the way up until my very last day with the Red Cross. As for the use of the Red Cross symbol, the only legal Red Cross in Bosnia-Herzegovina internationally recognised up until the war was the BH Red Cross, which had a cross as its universally recognised and acknowledged symbol. There was nothing that was questionable about the use of that symbol. As for international recognition by the International Red Cross, that did not occur pursuant to a request from the Sarajevo body back in 1993 when the request for recognition was first submitted; the reason being, that particular body did not exercise any control over the work of the various institutions throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nevertheless, the use of the symbol and cooperation with the International Committee of the Red Cross and the International Federation of the Red Cross and Red Crescent Society was never placed in doubt because of this situation that prevailed. It wasn't before the 15th of December, 2000, at an international conference of the International Red Cross that the BH Red Cross society was fully officially recognised. The following year at the general session, all the documents were adopted. On the 15th of December, rather, we held a founding assembly of this unified body for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then on the 8th of May, the Red Cross day the following year, the international recognition followed. It wasn't before then that these issues were resolved and the Red Cross symbol was confirmed and ratified as our national symbol, as well, although that symbol had up to then been used in all of the 169 local commune organisations that had been hard at work, although there was no unifying structure. In the Republika Srpska, you had the Republika Srpska Red Cross, which also submitted a request for international recognition; however, the response they got seven days later was that this was unfortunately impossible because their activities did not cover the entire territory of an internationally recognised country. The Red Cross of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna never submitted a request for international recognition to begin with. It was established only for the purpose of coordination in that particular area. What was required was an institutional response to all of the tasks that were arising after the law on the Red Cross of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna had been adopted. Cooperation with international societies of the Red Cross and the Red Crescent, the Budapest office and the new office that was established in Bosnia and Herzegovina was very good. Your humble servant actually had occasion to visit to Budapest office and all their other offices. I also had a chance to be involved in all of the activities surrounding the founding session in Geneva in 1999 as an observer. So as regards your question and the situation, this was something that was seriously considered, and this was fully under the control of the people who were involved with the work of the Red Cross. We were also aware of the fact that in some predominantly Muslim municipalities there was the Red Crescent, and they were active too. Nevertheless, they didn't have the required structure, and they never submitted any sort of individual request for any form of recognition whatsoever. Therefore, as I said yesterday, for purely humanitarian reasons and needs - and that was why they were around in the first place - we indicated the problem of their existence. Nevertheless, we believed that the aid that they as an organisation were providing was reason enough for us to not raise this as a problem or an issue. At the time they were working in the area, it was more important to get more aid rather than raise the issue of the symbol they were using because they weren't using their symbol officially. But since aid was coming in from that source, as well, we didn't mind, although we did in fact indicate this problem. All the institutions of the Red Cross were using one symbol and one symbol alone: the cross. Today it is still the cross. And now it is an internationally recognised association, a society in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. I would like to thank you, Mr. Simunovic, for your very argumented answer, and I would like to then say that it is what I also believed, that before 2000, that is before the international conference of the Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies in Geneva in 2000, your society like they are once in Bosnia and Herzegovina in a way acted in a de facto way without a final confirmation of the respective international bodies; but of course, you have done your work, and of course, then the official recognition came in 2000. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification on the record. Page 41, line 7 to 8. It wasn't caught on the transcript. I did hear on the translation. The gentleman indicated, and I will ask for a confirmation, where he said that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna never submitted any documentation for international recognition, is that correct, to the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct. We did not submit any request for international recognition, being as we were aware of the fact that we did not enjoy authority over the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and aware as we were of the fact that the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was an internationally recognised country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure we got that clarification. And one more point picking up on the question that was asked of you: The international Red Cross, the ICRC was on the ground in Mostar during 1992, 1993, monitoring and assisting your work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is certainly correct, but during the period of the most intense clashes they moved their office to Medjugorje. The rest of the time, we had worked directly with that institution. International Federation of the Red Cross and Red Crescent Associations only merged at a later stage, and they got in touch directly with these Red Cross organisations, including ours in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one point of detail. The Red Crescent was mentioned. I wanted to ask a question yesterday. We didn't have time for me to do so, so I'll put it straightaway. There was a Red Cross crescent, and there was also Merhamet. How did they both work? Did they work together, or were they rival organisations? I'm talking about the Red Crescent and Merhamet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the fact that upon obtaining membership in the coordinating committee both institutions are the representatives along with all the other humanitarian organisations, there was no competition in the sense of causing each other problems. There was a certain amount of rivalry in the sense of getting as much aid into the country as possible. As to their mutual relations outside the coordinating committee, I'm really not privy to that kind of detail. However, I did work with both these organisations, and our relations were good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And now let's go to the very last chapter. We'll be very brief on this. This has to do with the issue of public kitchens. It has come up before with one particular witness from the Prosecution, and I just want to get some of your testimony in regards to this. If we look at 1D 02773 -- do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it's dated 15 July 1992. We can see that this is on establishment of soup kitchens, conditions and criteria, and I take it you have looked at this -- you have looked at this document, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did you know the director, Mr. Enver Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us whether, indeed, at that time in Mostar there were soup kitchens?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to interpret this document a little. This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We were going to get to that step by step. First, you're going to -- so let me lead you with my questions, and then we'll get to the document. So the first general question: Were there soup kitchens? So were there soup kitchens at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are now, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could you describe so at least we have some sort of a mental picture of what a soup kitchen looked like and where they may have been at that time.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soup kitchens were set up in buildings where it was possible to prepare food in an organised way and where there was sufficient room for numbers of people to come and have a cooked meal. Sometimes, food that was cooked would be taken elsewhere outside the building itself. Certain locations were quite remote within the town itself, and some people who were in need of this sort of service would have been at too much of a risk going there on a daily basis to fetch their food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. How many meals a day were these soup kitchens cooking or providing?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the capacity of each of these and depending on their locations, the largest one was producing between 700 and 800 meals a day, and this is the one that was based at the Herzegovina restaurant, which enjoyed the best conditions, objectively speaking, for preparing an amount of food like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever eat in any of these soup kitchens to see the quality of the food?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please tell us, you know, how was it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chef would draw up a weekly plan of meals to be prepared. That plan was then followed, and humanitarian workers had this organisation scheme that we had and that we explained about yesterday in terms of distributing humanitarian aid, so this was then distributed. As for the basic supplies such as fresh meat or spices, which were the sort of staples that hardly ever arrived as humanitarian aid, this was something that was financed from the budget of the social welfare centre; and the social welfare centre was one of the co-founders of the soup kitchens. Each day, a warm meal would be cooked with the exception of Sundays when beneficiaries would be given some sort of a dry ration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned "chef," and I was going to ask you, who cooked these meals?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professional cooks who were employees of these soup kitchens. They were employees, as a matter of fact, of the social welfare centre and were under the supervision of all the sanitary institutions, the objective being to prevent any disease from spreading. They were under the supervision of all the other medical institutions, as well, when it came to the health and hygiene standards being applied to the food that they were preparing. In addition to those professional cooks, there were people there who helped with processing food stuffs in terms of preparing them for cooking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if I understood your previous answers, the Red Cross along with other organisations were providing some of the food stuffs that would be actually cooked at these soup kitchens. Is that -- did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Red Cross provided a quantity of flour to the bakeries on both sides in order to allow the soup kitchens to bake enough quantity of bread, and that was a daily obligation of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
