utterances.text: Did any of the international organisations such as UNHCR, ICRC complain of the fact that soup kitchens were being set up in order to feed the hungry and the needy?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Finally, before we get to the document, before we get there, my last question is, does someone have to qualify in order to go to the soup kitchen to receive a meal? Do they need some sort of a ration card, or could they just show up? What was the procedure, if you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to make an assumption of the daily number of beneficiaries to arrive, an assessment would be made of those who want or need to go to a soup kitchen, and a certain number of people had cards of soup kitchen beneficiaries; however, any soup kitchen was open for anyone who on that particular day had no other possibility of getting a meal. And this number accounted for perhaps 3 to 5 percent of the total number of users.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to the document. Now we're ready. 1D 02773. And if I may just point out a couple of things. You can see in the middle of the page that there are facilities on the right bank and on the left bank of the Neretva river. Can you confirm whether those kitchens were indeed in place at this time, because this document is dated 15 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them, yes, but some of them were just -- only being planned to be opened, so this document also contains an initiative for new ones to be opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you wanted to comment about this document. What else is it that strikes you about this document?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document, in my view, was a good basis for launching an important humanitarian initiative or category, and that is to ensure warm meals for the needy; and this initiative was welcomed by humanitarian organisations and the Red Cross. And from within the schedule of work of the coordinating committee, one can see that the soup kitchens were at the top of priority for providing locations and sites where people would receive aid. But that, of course, applied only to those locations that could be used for soup kitchens and preparation of food. As far as the work of soup kitchens is concerned, as I said earlier, they still exist in Mostar, one on the left bank and the other one on the right bank, although Mostar is not a divided town any longer, and they still have their beneficiaries. In other words, there are still needy people who do not have proper conditions for making or cooking their own meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we go on to the next document, and the next set of documents, actually, are sort of related or interrelated. 1D 02767. We see this one is dated 12 November 1993, and this is the social welfare centre, and we note the acting director is Marko Bevanda. I assume that you know this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mr. Bevanda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It says here in the very first paragraph: "By a decision of the Mostar municipality HVO approving the opening of a soup kitchen in Mostar, number 01-380/93 of 21 October 1993, a former facility of the Herzegovina GP construction company..." and it gives the address. Can you confirm whether, indeed, that soup kitchen opened and was operating?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at this address.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It then goes on to say that: "As this facility has no fixtures and fittings and we have information that the Herzegovina Hotel has fixtures and fittings that would serve this purpose, we hereby ask for your approval for the requisition of the fixtures and fittings necessary for the opening of a soup kitchen." Do you know the Herzegovina Hotel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which side is it, the left or the right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what sort of fixtures and fittings are they talking about, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the premises of GP Herzegovina, that is, their former canteen lacked chairs and tables. It also lacked big pots for cooking, and it was not a suitable area to open a soup kitchen. Therefore, the director of the social welfare centre addressed the bureau for economy of the municipality of Mostar to approve the use of the necessary equipment for the Hotel Herzegovina, which was not operating at the time, in order to establish the soup kitchen, and that is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And let's look at some of the other documents that would assist in that. 1D 02766 dated 16 November 1993. Here we see that there's an approval of the requisition of the necessary fixtures and fittings from the Herzegovina Hotel, and we see the header, "the economic office," a Vlado Bevanda. I take it you know this gentleman as well?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then going on to the next document, 1D 02765, this is 22 November 1993. This is from the acting director a Marko Bevanda writing: "We hereby ask you to approve the following tools and feeding items for the basic operation of the soup kitchen..." and we can see the various items, and this is to the Mostar IRC. Do you know what -- what is this -- who is this request to?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that's the international rescue committee, an organisation which was active in Mostar; but in its programme, it was not involved in providing humanitarian aid in food, but rather, helped by providing items that were needed to launch businesses and other economic facilities. So one could describe it more as providing something that was intended for reconstruction of the town to clean the facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And finally, 1D 02764. This is dated 8 December 1993. And here we have a report, and this -- have you had a chance to look at this report? This is, again, by the deputy director, Mr. Marko Bevanda.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this report only during an earlier preparation, but I know that all this was happening at the time and that it happened as described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it the soup kitchen functioned as it was expected to?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I was going to ask you -- that concludes this chapter. I was going to conclude my questioning by asking you about the events after 1994, post-Washington agreement, but I believe we covered that with Judge Prandler's question and you quite nicely told us about the continuing evolution of the Red Cross in Bosnia Herzegovina. So with that, I want to thank you very much, sir, for giving evidence at this stage, and we hope that you would be as forthcoming with the others as you have been with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I would also like to thank you for leading this part nicely, and I thank to all of you who asked me questions in this introductory section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now address the second part and hear Defence counsel representing the other accused. Since Mr. Karnavas has had three hours, so you will half an hour and a half. I don't know how you are going to share your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Simunovic. On behalf of General Praljak's Defence team, I would like to ask you few questions for the information of the Chamber, and pursuant to the decision of the Chamber, I'm referring you to a document that was used by Dr. Prlic's Defence team, and that's document 1D 02761, which was mentioned on pages 68 and 69 of the record of yesterday's session, as well as on page 89 of the record, line 9, where mention was made of family cards and individuals who took care of those cards. Mr. Simunovic, you have the set of documents in front of you, and I would kindly ask you to look at document 3D 03178. You would agree with me that this is a family card similar to the one that we saw yesterday and that was issued by the Rodoc local commune?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This card refers to the Strelcevina local commune?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Will the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This local commune covers the centre of the town, and it is a pretty large local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. I'm going to repeat the question because due to the pace the question was not recorded in the transcript. My question was, what was the area covered by Strelcevina local commune. Strelcevina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just been warned that according to the transcript, it seems that his honour Judge Antonetti is leading this examination, and that was recorded on page 51, line 16; therefore, I would like the transcript to be corrected in the sense that this examination is being led Nika Pinter. Mr. Simunovic, can we now go through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that I ask a great many questions, but you shouldn't attribute to me questions that I haven't asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, especially if you do not agree with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let us now go through this card. On the left-hand side, it reads what the nationality of the recipient of the aid is. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We see that is he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That he is teacher?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And also listed are his family members?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: They were all receiving humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Who filled out these cards?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Government commissioners for a specific local commune after they conducted the procedure that I described earlier in cooperation with the social welfare centre and humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: As we can see, this first card refers to a person who is a Muslim by ethnicity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it reads.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: On the next page, we see the dates indicating what?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first column on the left indicates the type of the aid received, and it's stated in codes. If we recall what we spoke about yesterday, this was the list that was put up as public notices in local communes, and it's indicated that the distribution took place. The column on the right contains the dates, when the distribution actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Therefore, this is not the date until which the distribution was provided but actually the date when it was delivered. Can you now look at document 3D 03227, which comprises of a number of documents, and these are family cards as well. However, on the first one, we see that it was issued in the Zahum local commune?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what these dates on the front cover indicate?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These dates indicate the dates when this card was certified or confirmed by the social welfare centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This family card was held by a Muslim person according to the details there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Palandzic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Will the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So this is the Zahum local commune?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This is a different street now, isn't it? This street is 8 Dzuka [phoen], number 4, right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Is there a such a street in Mostar? Dzika [phoen], Dzuka?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The English interpretation will resume once the speakers have been kindly reminded to observe a pause. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the address is 8 Dalmatian, Assault, Corps. It's an acronym.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you go back to the first file, please. What address is this?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilicka 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Is this a street?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please go to the next file now. Zahum again. The person in question, Nusret Suta?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, Asim Duka, 8, right? The street?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Again, the date aid was received, right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And number of other files that we have here. Can you please go to the one where it says "beneficiary, Ljubo Barasic."

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Oh, you have. Great. According to the information contained in this file, he seems to be an ethnic Croat?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And we see that he was also receiving aid at almost the same time intervals, right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking, without considering the detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But all this can be checked, right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And you can confirm for our benefit that these files were issued to all those who were entitled to receive these family files?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Fine. Can you now just leaf through these documents and tell me if they're all in reference to these family cards or files that we have been speaking about over the last two days? The commissioners filled them out; and based on these, people received humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The same procedure applied throughout Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you now please open 3D 03249. Again, this is a set of files of family cards. Can you please just briefly skim through them. Have a look and tell us if this is in reference to Mostar. And can you confirm that these are the same kind of files?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are two major streets, Stjepan Radic Street and Vladimir Nazor Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Zoric Street as well. That's what I see here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Fine. May I, therefore, conclude that we have a copy in front of us of authentic files that were issued to citizens of Mostar back in 1992 and 1993? You are able to confirm that for me, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, no problem. I can confirm that for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Having looked at these family files recording the dates on which humanitarian aid was received as well as the persons who were the recipients, can you agree with the conclusion that in terms of distributing humanitarian aid, the Muslims were at no disadvantage whatsoever? They were in no way kept from receiving humanitarian aid, were they? They were in fact receiving humanitarian aid under the same conditions and under the same terms as the Croats, right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to confirm this the other way around. They were receiving aid under the same conditions, on the same terms. They were in no way at a disadvantage as far as receiving aid was concerned. If you look at the record, you will see that they were real beneficiaries of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This concludes my cross-examination. Just for purposes of information, I would like to say that information in relation to the family files is information that was taken from a document or a CD that has the following number: 3D 03151 and 3D 03152. This is a database, and the documents that were presented are mere samples, standing for dozens and hundreds of family files contained in those CDs. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for the witness. Could you look at document 3D 03227 on page 3D 361611 and 3D 361612. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in reference to Halil Pintula, if I may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Halil Pintula.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm interested in are stamps on all these cards. On the first page, even though it's not very legible, the stamps are stamps that belong to who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I look at the files that I have, and they have been presented already, 1D 02761 and the rest that we've been looking at, the stamp above, or rather, in this case Halil Pintula, the right upper corner, is the social welfare centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, please turn the page and you will see a stamp, which I believe is the stamp of the Red Crescent. 1612.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that, but it's quite illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can see a crescent. You agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have a clearer view on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the fact that there is a stamp of the Red Crescent, would this mean that this social welfare centre and the Red Crescent were working together because the stamps are used on the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Red Crescent as an organisation was a member of the coordinating committee for collection and distribution of humanitarian aid. It is quite possible that this particular person at this point in time received his or her own allocation of aid on the premises of the Red Crescent. This individual went on an individual basis to the Red Crescent. They brought their file along and got some sort of aid. The date was subsequently recorded, all this handover of aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which would explain why there is a stamp of the Red Crescent here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aid was distributed in this case on the premises of the humanitarian organisation known as the Red Crescent, and this is something that I omitted earlier on. Sometimes aid was distributed on the very premises occupied by these various humanitarian organisations, especially in relation to some -- the peculiar types of aid, orthopedic braces and tools, aids, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe my colleague has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please look at the card on document 1D 002761. 1D 002761. Please look at document -- the document which we've been shown awhile ago, 3D 003249. We have two different cards; and like our Presiding Judge, I'm interested in the stamps. On the first document, 1D 002761, I see the stamp which is the stamp of the Serb brigade of the HVO, 9th battalion; and on the other cards which were shown to us by Ms. Pinter, we have no stamps of any brigade whatsoever. I don't know if you can give us an explanation for this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I can. In this particular local commune, they recorded something else in these files, too, namely who the members were of the military units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I've understood you correctly, the family who was the beneficiary was a family of military people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are to understand this properly, there are HVO soldiers who did not have enough to eat, and they had to resort to the social welfare centre in order to get aid, various forms of aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One could put it that way, but the reason for any file to be issued was the social conditions under which an entire family, for example, was living. I happen to know this very family. The husband is an invalid. They had every right to be on this list for aid distribution. These are cards and files from the local commune of which I am a native; therefore, I know all of these people personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one correction. I believe the gentleman said the wife of the -- the wife is the invalid, not the husband.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's the wife. The husband is called Ahmo. Is that right? What's the husband's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ahmo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the husband was a member of the Serb brigade of the 9th battalion, of the HVO; is that right? He was a member of the Serb brigade. There was an error on the transcript. I can't check the transcript and listen to what the witness is saying. So he was a member of the HVO. Now, what you are saying is interesting because if I look at the date, 6th of March, 1993; 7th of April, 1993; 18th of August, 1993; 16th of September, 1993; 28th of October, 1993; 18th of December, 1993; 1st of February, 1994. That soldier, that HVO soldier, was he a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he wasn't arrested, was he? He wasn't captured by the HVO, was he, and taken prisoner since he receives the aid throughout the year 1993? So he was still a member of the HVO unit, I understand. As far as you know, did a lot of the Muslims remain? A great many or just a few? What percentage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say. I can't talk about the percentage, but I know that there were those who remained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's sometimes a small detail like this one that one is able to understand things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Apparently, his answers are not getting into the transcript because he's confirmed it. He said, yes, yes, this was earlier. Now, I don't know whether it's not being translated or it's not being picked up because of the court reporter. I just wanted to point that out, and of course, the gentleman would have to affirm those answers as opposed to shaking the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, witness. Please say it again. This Muslim soldier remained in an HVO unit because it's not been recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simunovic, my name is Vesna Alaburic. I'm an attorney at law from Zagreb, and along with my learned friend Nicholas Stewart, an attorney from London, I defend General Milivoj Petkovic. Witness, have we ever met? This is for the Chamber to be able to judge my examination of you as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Since we haven't met, we've had no opportunity to discuss this case as a result. Let me ask you questions now that only have to do with the answers you provided yesterday when asked about your visit to Heliodrom, about the clash of the 9th of May, 1993. I will quote certain portions of your answers to you, and then we'll take one step at a time and analyse your answers. If need be, I will be showing you certain documents and confronting you with previous statements about these circumstances. If I'm not mistaken, you say that you lived near Heliodrom and you're quite familiar with the area, right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the clash on the 9th of May, 1993? How many times did you visit Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about what occurred on the 9th of May. There were civilians that were captured there. They were released on or about the 18th of May, so I'm talking about the nine or ten days. How many times did you visit Heliodrom throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at least three times, but the first day was my longest stay there, or visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say the first day, you mean the 9th of May, right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Karnavas asked you a question yesterday. This is at page 61, lines 3 and 4. I'll quote in English. [In English] At some point you were asked to be to the Heliodrom on or about May 9. [Interpretation] You answered affirmatively. Who asked you to go to Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to Heliodrom having previously learned about the situation that had come about involving the people who were inside. I can't specifically remember right now whether there was such a thing as an open invitation by anyone for me to come. I do know, however, that I went there as soon as I had arrived in town and as soon as I'd learned about the situation and the developments at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you were asked this question that I quoted. Does that not mean that your answer should be negative because no one had ever asked you to actually go and visit Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Later on in response to some questions - and again, the pages are 19, 20 and 21 - you say you learned what had actually happened. You go on to say that a number of people that same night were put up at Heliodrom. Mr. Simunovic, what exactly was it that you learned had happened on the 9th of May in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that a lot of people from the town itself because of the war had been moved to Heliodrom. I saw more of that later on when I watched TV footage, more than I had witnessed myself at the time I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If my understanding is right, you actually received information that certain people who were living along the confrontation line had now been moved to Heliodrom for security-related reasons. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your assumption only as soon as I arrived at the scene. I was a humanitarian worker, and all I knew at the time was that some people had been put up there. A considerable number of people, perhaps I should say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who shared that with you, the fact that people had been put up at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to trace this information back to its source now. I was with the Red Cross, and all those who were living in Mostar at the time knew about what was going on, but I was living in Radoc, and I had no idea. I had a different approach to information, generally speaking, rather, different access to information that than the people who were living in Mostar itself. When I met some people that morning, everybody was talking about that and the situation that had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What time of day was it, roughly speaking, on the 9th of May when you reached Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may have been at about 10.00 a.m. or thereabouts. I first drove into town and then back, so this would take a total of about two hours, roughly speaking, the round trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many buildings were there at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you include the former aviation school, then there were quite many buildings there. I would perhaps require some time to do the math because there's this main street on the way in, and then there are buildings either side of that road. And of course, there's a parallel street with yet more buildings that were previously used for the purposes of the aviation academy that at the time belonged to the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday at page 63, lines 19 and 20, that you walked up to this building where the military command was, quoted. As far as I understand, that was the only building you ever went to, right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you went a total of three times, and that was the only building you ever went to. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the warden was, the deputy warden and all the other officials who were in charge of the Heliodrom prison?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first person I was in touch was a man named Stanko. I think his last name was Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember what he was?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, you mean his position? I think he was in charge of logistics or security or something or other. Later on, I met Mr. Josip, as well, who was a logistician or whatever. Anyway, there were these two persons that I spoke to about their needs and what the Red Cross might provide in terms of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at this other gentleman who you say was called Josip. Can you perhaps remember his last name? Josip Praljak, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Karnavas asked you whether you were in touch with anyone who was in charge of coordinating all the activities going on at Heliodrom, and your answer was that you were in touch with the officer who was in charge of logistics in those buildings. This is at pages 62 and 63 and then lines 22 through the bottom of that page 62 and the first three lines on page 63. So you were in touch with the chief officer in charge of logistics in those buildings. Can you tell us the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only ever in touch with two persons there, the persons that I mentioned a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was any of them wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were both wearing uniforms, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was either of them or both of them, as far as you know, members of any military unit of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did either of them or both of them tell you about what was happening at Heliodrom, why these people were being kept there, what were the plans about these people?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically, we only talked and discussed how we can help these people. There were many people there. I still -- up to this date, I don't know how many people were there, and the longest conversation was about one hour and one and a half hours, and it was focused on what they needed for their kitchen and what we were able to supply to them. We didn't tackle any other issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So can you please confirm once again that apart from contacting Mr. Bozic and Mr. Josip Praljak, you did not have any contact with anyone else in Heliodrom and discuss the conditions prevailing there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question arising from Ms. Alaburic's question. You met with two people in charge of Heliodrom, Mr. Stanko Bozic and Mr. Josip Praljak. You met them for humanitarian questions. You wanted to know what kind of assistance you could provide since your mission was to provide assistance. Earlier on, you said that there were a lot of people. You didn't know exactly how many. It's very interesting because you first saw Mr. Bozic; did he give you the impression that he didn't know anything about the situation that prevailed and that he was, therefore, unable to tell you whether he needed 1.000, 2.000, 5.000, or 10.000 meals because he could not forecast the future; or was your impression that he knew that those people were going to stay there for quite some time and he may have asked you to make sure you could provide some kind of follow-up logistics for some time? What was your impression? Did he seem to be overwhelmed by the events? Did he seem to not to know at all how those people were going to stay there, in what condition, or did he come across at somebody who was very organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, it is difficult to recall the whole situation given the panic that was also enveloping me. The quantity of aid that the Red Cross at the time was able to provide gave me concern, and I was really worried to what extent I would be able to respond to their requirements. That is why I remained for only a short while and then went back to the Red Cross to check what we had available. I believe that Mr. Bozic, as well, who was the first one who I met, was also concerned about how we would be able to provide help and assistance to such a large number of people. When he saw me, he was somewhat relieved. However, our response in terms of humanitarian aid was not an adequate one because we didn't have available goods on stock, and that was perhaps the reason why I didn't go there many times afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were not able to help him much because you did not have much in your warehouses. That's what you just said, isn't it? But at your level, did you think you could try and contact international organisations that were present on the ground for them to take care of the logistical problem because you were not able to? But the organisational level had everything they needed. They can organise air lifts. They have means and resources. Did you think of such a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you put it very nicely; however, the response of international organisations in such situations was not as rapid as one would have expected. They had their respective warehouses most often located outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For supplying aid in wartimes, they requested extra security from international army units in order to be able to pass through in a secure way, and this issue could not have been settled in three or five days. I sent out an appeal to the Red Cross organisations in the neighbouring countries [as interpreted], and there was some response, but the situation that we can see from these reports could not have been resolved within ten days by which time many people had left. I think that the major role in providing these people with aid was the HVO reserve because there were no other organisations present there. We were primarily concerned with hygiene and to a lesser extent with food because we didn't have sufficient food as I explained yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just two technical points. I believe the gentleman didn't say "neighbouring countries" but "neighbourhood." By that -- I'm told that he must have meant or would have meant neighbouring municipalities. And also further down, he mentioned --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I meant municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where it says "HVO reserves," the gentleman indicated HVO logistics. Perhaps you could confirm that he said logistics as opposed to HVO reserves. It does make a difference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently, there was a problem. You mentioned logistics and the reserves the HVO may have had. So if one is to understand properly, you realised there were problems, but you did not have the means to solve them. Is that a possible conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is a possible conclusion, not to resolve it completely. We responded to the extent that we were able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now we've got the other Defence team. We've had [Realtime transcript read in error, "2D"] 3D, 4D, now 5D.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wanted to suggest that since we are nearly at the time for a break to take one now, and I will distribute binders to the interpreters' booths, and then after that we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. I said we had 3D, 4D, 5D. I didn't mention 2D. I can see there's 2D on line 3, page 70. Ms. Nozica, I'm not mistaken. You didn't say anything, did you?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I would like to greet everyone in this courtroom. We are getting up out of according to our normal sequence. The first one was 3D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Defence counsel, you have the floor, but there's always somebody missing. The witness is not in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like just to advise the Chamber that during the break we consulted with our client, Mr. Coric, and on his suggestion we are not going to cross-examine this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Pusic's Defence is following your instruction when it comes to questioning the contacts with the accused, and in that sense we decided not to conduct any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Nozica, you are the last Defence counsel, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. For the record, I would like to say that the testimony of this witness does not refer to Mr. Bruno Stojic in any way, but I would like to ask him a few questions about the things that he apparently has knowledge of it. This is going to be a cross-examination that will deal with only one issue. I would like to the witness to try and explain to us on the basis of the document that is prepared already in the binder which facilities at Heliodrom the witness visited on the 9th of May, or rather, can the witness try and identify these facilities for us. I would like to note that we had attempted to do this with another witness before during the Prosecution case, but we were not lucky enough to have a witness who was able to identify this. However, we have today a witness who claims to have been at Heliodrom, and I suppose he will be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Simunovic.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My name is Senka Nozica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, I have just had a quick look at your document. You could have included some photographs unless the photographs have already been downloaded in the e-court system. Now, if you need to recognise something, it's better to have photographs, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for this suggestion. We do have photographs in the documents that were supplied to us by the Prosecution. However, I would like to ask the witness to do the identification on this map. This is another Prosecution document. If we put it on ELMO, I would kindly ask him to mark the facility that he visited on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, sir, as I told you, my name is Senka Nozica, along with my colleague Karim Khan represent Mr. Stojic in this trial. Will you please look at this document that's 2D 00136 [Realtime transcript read in error, "0016"]. This is the only document that was given to you, and I would like to ask the usher to put the last sheet of this document on the ELMO, the last page, and I'm going to ask you to try, since on page 2 of this document you have -- or rather page 3, you have an explanation of what represents what. I haven't shown you this document before; is that right? Sir, first tell me, have I ever had any contact with you, to make it clear for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in relation to this story, but we did meet during our travels.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. You are younger than I am, and I'm glad that you haven't forgotten it, but we never met concerning this issue. Can you please tell me, can you find your bearings in this map, this layout of the former HVO barracks, and it also says "the Heliodrom concentration camp." And I would like to repeat once again for the record that this is an OTP document. Can you please look at these numbers and the list of all the facilities. I would like to hear which of these facilities you visited on the 9th of May and where you met Mr. Bozic and Mr. Praljak as you said. And my second question is, according to what you know, where these detainees were kept in these facilities.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I find it difficult to orientate myself with this document since I cannot see any markings 1, 2, et cetera, except for those ones that are larger and which are outside the border of the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, can you please try with what you had on the side, and it has been enlarged on the screen. You can see what is written there, kitchen, command, school, sports hall, and beneath it said "SVZ."

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only in this facility marked "command."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So that's the facility, and the usher will help you. Can you just mark this building. Put a circle around it and put number 1. The first one is "command" from left to right, it's handwritten; "kitchen," and above that -- I see where your pencil is, so there it is. Can you please -- if that is the facility in question, can you mark it and just put a line on the side and a figure 1.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So for the record, we can say that this is the command building which you visited. If possible, can you tell us, did you know in what other facilities and buildings civilians were being kept at the time? If you cannot identify them on this layout sketch, do you know at least how these facilities were called and what was their previous usage at the time when this was a JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know where they were, these people who were there. While this was a JNA barracks, we as children were strictly forbidden to access it; therefore, I'm more familiar with the former air force high school than the military compound itself, which at the time was separated from the high school.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: After or before this event, did you ever come to this area following the departure of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never went there to inspect the facility and look at it. I very rarely went to that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did Mr. Bozic or Mr. Praljak tell you where the persons who were brought there, in a way for their own protection, were being kept?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember them mentioning any specific buildings, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Under number 1 that you have put, can you put today's date - I believe it's the 21st of October, 2008 - and sign it, please. And I would like to get an IC number for this layout, and with this I've finished. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The diagram shall be given Exhibit number IC 00869 [Realtime transcript read in error, "00369"]. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a small follow-up question. Ms. Nozica wanted you to recognise the buildings, and I understand that so many years later, it's a tall task for you. As far as you recollect, Witness, when you got there and arrived in your car, did you have to pass a military checkpoint, or were there soldiers standing at the entrance, or were you able to get straight to the buildings? If you remember, of course. I understand if you don't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only passed through the checkpoint at the very gate of the compound. This is at the far right where this road ends. So that is the last point on the right, and that's the road leading beneath these buildings that are marked black. This is where the gatehouse was and where access to the building was, and this is still a gatehouse where people enter this compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the checkpoint, both you and I when we did our military service, we had to pass checkpoints. The soldiers that were there, did they have to refer to their superiors before letting you go by? Did they check your papers, or did they ask you to wait? What did they actually do, and did they have to wait to see what they needed to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since, Your Honour, I was in a marked vehicle, and since I was a person known to people in the town, I didn't have any problems gaining access. I only explained the reason for my visit, and I was allowed to pass through without any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, the soldiers knew you. Since you had a vehicle with markings on it, it's true that the enemy can enter in disguise. You were able to enter because they recognised you; is that right? Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a little intervention. On page 72, line 12, I called up document 2D 00136, whereas the transcript reflects 2D 0016; and my colleague is also reminding me that IC number is also incorrect. That's on page 74. According to my records, it should be 8. Probably, we have passed 369 a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. My name is --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: My name is Miguel Longone, and I will conduct the cross-examination on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, before starting with the cross-examination, yesterday was an issue raised with the witness regarding some names of ICRC and Red Cross workers that the witness has been in contact with during the war, and I wanted to ask the Trial Chamber whether they want me to name those people to refresh the recollection of the witness in closed session or...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is better to mention the names in private session since measures have been granted. It's better to move into private session. Registrar, can we move into private session for a few moments, please. Mr. Longone, do we have any documents? I have nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Mr. Simunovic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Yesterday, we were referring to the principles of the Red Cross -- of the MUP, not the Red Cross. And in that respect, we were referring to which were the principles of that movement. Do you remember that? You mentioned that the aim of the Red Cross was to protect and to assist all the victims of the conflict, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And the principles that they follow in order to protect those victims of the conflict, all of them, were based on humanity?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Solidarity, unity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And humanity?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Humanity, solidarity, unity, neutrality, and there's one more, but I can't remember it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Do you remember the word "impartiality"?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: So impartiality was another one of the principles, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And there's a Bosnia regional Red Cross, and certainly, the Herceg-Bosna Red Cross of Mostar agree to respect and apply these principles in their work, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that you've misspoken. There was no Bosnian Red Cross in Mostar. There was a municipal Red Cross organisation in Mostar, which was part of the Red Cross of Herceg-Bosna. And if you allow me, I would like this to be accurately stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: I would ask you again the question. Did the regional Herceg-Bosna Red Cross and the Herceg-Bosna Red Cross of Mostar apply the principles of the Red Cross movement that we discussed just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, sir, that the work of the Red Cross in times of conflict is to make respect agreement regarding specially the safe passage of humanitarian assistance?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Cross was in a different position. The Red Cross was to be provided with safe passage of humanitarian aid by the authorities in charge and not vice-versa, for the Red Cross to ensure secure and safe passage; and on all ID cards of members of the Red Cross, it states that safe and free passage should be guaranteed and participation in activities. It was not, therefore, the Red Cross that secured the traffic; rather, others on the basis of the conventions were supposed to provide that for the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: It would be the government that was in charge?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police, and some services that have been established, and if there was some kind of congestion and other institutions with their security services. In one word, all the institutions that the Red Cross member would come across, once they show their ID -- Red Cross ID, representatives of these institutions were supposed to let them pass through provided they have a valid reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And if those principles were not respected or their work was stopped, you would request, actually, to let -- your mandate to be executed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that eventuality, we would send a report to the International Committee of the Red Cross and the local authorities or whoever was responsible in a certain institution or the superiors of whoever stood in the way of the Red Cross, given, of course, the fact that the Red Cross people had a good reason to want to be let through.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And one other of the works of the Red Cross was not only regarding a humanitarian system but to have access to prisoners and to assess their condition, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this mandate is something that is determined only for -- by the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And in this respect, sir, if we can go to the Exhibit that you discussed with the Defence in your direct examination, 1D 02434. It's in the Prosecution binder, in the first binder. Do you have it with you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And in this respect, sir, you see there is a representative of the regional Red Cross and the Red Cross of Mostar that signed an agreement in Geneva on the 8 May 1992, isn't it? If you see page 1D 51-0468 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I am afraid I don't understand what you're saying. Can you please repeat that for my benefit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: That the agreement regarding those principles of the Red Cross and the work of the Red Cross, the regional Red Cross and the Red Cross of Mostar of the Herceg-Bosna regional Red Cross, were signed by a representative of them in Geneva on the 8th of May, 1992; and the name of that person is in the page I have indicated to you, 1D 51 -0468?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that person's name on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: There are four persons mentioned in that agreement. Number 3, do you recognise the name of Mr. Sito Coric, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Could you please read what it says beside Sito Coric?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] President of Croatian Democratic Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Miljenko Brkic [phoen] was the representative of the Red Cross - the regional Red Cross back in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Miljenko Brkic was president of the Croatian Democratic Party, community, party at the time. It was on his behalf that he signed this and was actually present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, if you can please look at -- so you are saying that Mr. Sito Coric was not representing the regional Red Cross at that time? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he said he doesn't recognise the name of Mr. Coric. The question was quite clear, and the answer, also, was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Mr. Sito Coric was a member of the regional Red Cross of Herceg-Bosna, sir, in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my esteemed Prosecutor. I'm reading this document in front of me. Mr. S. Coric was the representative of Mr. Miljenko Brkic. There is nothing here that has anything to do with the Red Cross. In addition to that, I have no idea what you are asking me. I might be able to imagine how he placed Mr. Brkic in this context, but more about that later, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: I don't want to you imagine anything, sir. Let's focus on Exhibit 1D 02433 dated 20 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you repeat that number?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: You have your translation, sir, under the B/C/S. I think it's under the English. The B/C/S and the English are together in that document, is it? Have you find the translation under the same document? Yes. If you go further you will see, I think, a translation in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, no, I apologise. No, I've got a different document now. Just a second, please. [English] I have not the translation for this document. But it's not the same document. It's not translation of this. I know English. That is absolutely different document. Different ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Right. Did you see, sir, at the end of that document who the regional Red Cross of Herceg-Bosna is appointed as its representative in Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's a misrepresentation of the document. I suggest the gentleman read it correctly. Who is he representing, the interest of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ. That's why the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir? Would you please -- sir, would you please read the last paragraph of that document, the regional -- starting "The regional Red Cross of the Herceg-Bosna community appoints..." Will you please continue with that sentence, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Authorised representative in Switzerland regional Red Cross of the HZ Herceg-Bosna hereby appoints Mr. Simon Sito Coric." And I, by your leave, have never seen this document before. I wasn't with the Red Cross at the time, and I was not familiar with these kinds of powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, the document that we were discussing before is from Geneva. You mentioned that you started to work in June 1992 with the Red Cross, with the Herceg-Bosna Red Cross, isn't it? That was your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is I started working with the Mostar Red Cross in late June; and after I came to that position, I became familiar with the activities of the regional Red Cross of Herceg-Bosna at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And, sir, you said that you knew the principles of the movement of the Red Cross, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: You have to get familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: You have to read agreements, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The agreement was never in the archive of my Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you have read the statutes and the agreements of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the statute and the booklet with the mandates of the international movement of the Red Cross. To a large extent, they were adopted by this agreement. Then I had looked at the agreement with the Defence team. The first time I laid eyes on this document was during my proofing by the Defence but not before that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And in that agreement, if we go back, now, then, to the agreement of 2, 1992, that we were previously discussing, exhibit 1D 02434, Mr. Sito Coric was representing the regional Herceg-Bosna Red Cross in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Longone, I would really like to say that, first of all, the number of the exhibit had not been listed here in the transcript; so therefore, please kindly repeat that number. And another remark of mine is that you, both of you, you are overlapping each other, and please kindly slow down, both of you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I repeat the exhibit number that we were discussing previously, 1D 02434.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: You have it with you now?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And there in page 2 of that exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but in 1D 0234 [sic] there are a couple of documents. Which one the Prosecutor is referring to now specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: I was referring to the -- I will give you the page. 1D 51-0469.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And how can you be sure that the witness is looking to proper one if he is not given the sub-number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Witness, did you find the page?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that the action plan signed and agreed by the regional Red Cross Herceg-Bosna was according with the aim of the International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What action plan are you talking about? This is a plan by the International Committee of the Red Cross, ICRC. [In English] It's not plan for international -- local Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, if we go to page 1D 51-0477 of that exhibit. You see the signature of Sito Coric, a representative of the regional Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he keeps saying the representative of the regional Red Cross. Where does it say that is he a representative of the regional Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: We have seen that the regional Red Cross appointed Mr. Simon Sito Coric as his authorised representative in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the signature of Sito Coric on that page?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to ask you, though, to go to 1D 570101 at the very beginning of the transcript so you see what the respective capacities of participants in this meeting were. It reads here, representative of the HZD -- representatives of the HDZ. The HDZ was represented by at that meeting Mr. Coric -- Saric [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: He was representing the regional Red Cross in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is simply not alleged by this document. I do apologise, but I think we are just going around in circles with no need at all. We are fusing, as it were, two documents that are really not from the same source, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, let's go to Exhibit 1D 02655 from the Defence. 1D 02655. That's the statute of the regional Red Cross of the Herceg-Bosna community.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: In Article 2 of that statute, on page 2, it says that the regional Red Cross is a voluntary humanitarian organisation.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. Shall I go on reading it, or will you oblige?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Respond my answers. Article 2 says that the regional Red Cross is a constituent part of the Red Cross of Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And that was on the 20 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Article 3 states that the regional Red Cross consists of municipal Red Cross organisations, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And that the main objective or among the purpose of work if we see -- if we go to page 3 of the same document, if you see in Article 8, is to ensure preservation of peace among people, among the purposes of their work.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in keeping with international principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: In Article 9 of the following page, to assist victims in armed conflicts?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Which bullet?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: To take part in organising and providing social, medical, and material aid. Do you see that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why not point to the right -- you know, just say. Which one is it? Make it easy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Point 7. Under Article 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Third from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Did you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And the following -- the following bullet point it says is to collect, organise, keep, and provide the data on victims of armed conflicts?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And carry out other activities of tracing service?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot interpret a witness who keeps talking in two different languages at the same time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, sir. It was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Simunovic, the interpreters would like to ask you to use only one language because you sometimes speak Croatian, and sometimes you speak English, and it is very difficult for them to follow you. And also, I ask you again to be really a bit slowing down more because it is a very difficult question and to also to name the very paragraphs or mention the very paragraphs about which you would like to ask the witness to speak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I am still waiting for a question from the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor is asking me to read the text. Is that really necessary? If so, I'll just oblige and I'll read this text, which by the way has already been recorded and translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that the regional Red Cross and the Red Cross of Mostar among the basic programatic tasks had to collect, organise, keep, and provide the data on victims of armed conflicts and carry out other activities of a tracing service?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And they have to inform - that's the following bullet point - they have to inform citizens with human rights stemming from the Geneva Conventions and additional protocols with the conventions and to inform citizens about them?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. We did that, too, whenever we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And if we go to page 5 of the same article, of the same exhibit, you have Article 13, and there is a structure of the Herceg-Bosna regional Red Cross. You have the basic Red Cross organisation, the municipal Red Cross organisations, and the original Red Cross. Could you please indicate, were -- the Herceg-Bosna Red Cross from Mostar that you were belonged to that you were the president, where in this category you will put that Mostar Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Mostar Red Cross was a municipal organisation of the Red Cross. It comprised basic organisations of the Red Cross in schools, local communities, and other areas throughout Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: If we can go now to 1D 02660.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And if we can see -- at the bottom of Article 2, do you recognise the statute, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Is your signature at the front of the statute?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: So this is a statute of the Mostar municipal Herceg-Bosna Red Cross, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And Article 2 of that statute, in page 2 at the bottom, it says that the regional -- that the Red Cross of Mostar is part of the regional Red Cross, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It reads that the municipal organisation was part of the Red Cross of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And the Red Cross of the republic of Herceg-Bosna, was that the original Red Cross, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, yes, but then later it became what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, one of the reasons you mentioned the creation of the regional Red Cross of Mostar and the local Red Cross was a broken communications, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would really like to ask you one thing. Don't keep linking the regional Red Cross and the Mostar Red Cross all the time. There was no regional Mostar Red Cross. There was the regional Red Cross of Herceg-Bosna and the municipal Red Cross in Mostar, and that's what all the documents say. And that's just for ease of understanding, and that's why I would like to kindly ask you to keep the two terms apart, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: Sir, the local Red Cross of Herceg-Bosna from Mostar was part of the regional Red Cross of Herceg-Bosna, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipal Red Cross of Mostar was part of the regional Red Cross of Herceg-Bosna and later part of the Red Cross of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And you said in the beginning of your testimony that the regional Red Cross and the Red Cross of Mostar, the Herceg-Bosna one, so the Herceg-Bosna regional Red Cross and the Herceg-Bosna Red Cross from Mostar were an integral part of the Red Cross from Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it? That's what you said in the beginning of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipal Mostar Red Cross was part of the Red Cross of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the regional Red Cross of Herceg-Bosna up until the establishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. After that, the municipal Mostar Red Cross was only part of the Red Cross of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna because at the federal level the Red Cross did not function and could not perform these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: And if we move to Exhibit 1D 2661 -- do you have the exhibit with you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
utterances.text: There were some questions about whether -- about the neutrality and impartiality and independence of the regional Red Cross or the Herceg-Bosna Red Cross, as you want to name it. And would you agree with me, sir, that in October 1994 the Herceg-Bosna Red Cross was not anymore in a humanitarian organisation and non-governmental one but a state humanitarian organisation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONGONE
